en: Magma beneath Mount Makiling heats underground water into steam, which spins turbines to generate geothermal electricity for nearby provinces.
Warm Pacific Ocean waters evaporate to fuel massive rotating storms, causing frequent typhoons to strike the eastern coasts.
Tiny coral polyps in Tubbataha Reef extract calcium carbonate from seawater to build hard skeletons, gradually forming massive reef structures.
The Cagayan River slows down as it reaches the sea, dropping carried sediments to gradually build a wide, fertile delta.
The Sierra Madre mountain range blocks moist Pacific winds, dropping heavy rain on the east while leaving central plains drier.
Massive volcanic eruptions at Taal collapsed the ground into a large caldera, which later filled with rainwater to form the lake.
Dense mangrove roots in Panguil Bay trap flowing sediments and break ocean wave energy, effectively preventing severe coastal soil erosion.
Slightly acidic rainwater slowly dissolved the underlying limestone rock over millions of years, carving the massive Puerto Princesa Subterranean River cave.
Gravity channels mountain spring water through ancient bamboo pipes, flooding the cascading Ifugao Rice Terraces to irrigate the growing crops.
Uplifted marine limestone in Bohol eroded from heavy rainfall over thousands of years, shaping the distinct conical Chocolate Hills.
The thick forest canopy of Mount Apo intercepts heavy rain, allowing water to slowly seep into soil and feed downstream springs.
The collision of the Eurasian and Philippine Sea plates pushed molten rock upward, forming the archipelago's volcanic islands.
